title: Seeds: how a seed grows into a new plant

summary.text: Plant a chana seed, and for days nothing shows above the soil. But under the soil, the seed is busy. A seed is a tiny living plant, and when the seed gets water, the seed grows a root first, down into the soil. Then a shoot comes up into the light. Your child plants five chana seeds and gently digs one up each day to see what is happening underneath.
summary.art: A cup of soil cut away like a cross-section, showing a chana seed with a long white root going down and a small curled shoot just reaching the top of the soil.

intro.hook: Hold a dry chana seed. Is this hard little ball alive? Could a whole plant come out of this seed?
intro.text: Many plants you know, from the tulsi on the balcony to the big neem tree on the road, began as a seed. Seeds look like small stones. But put a seed in damp soil, and a new plant grows out of the seed. In this unit we plant seeds and watch. We also peek under the soil, to find out what a seed does before we can see anything.
intro.art: A child's open palm holding a few dry chana seeds, with a pot of tiny green chana plants in front.

outcomes: By the end I can say that a seed grows into a new plant.
By the end I can say what a seed needs to start growing: water.
By the end I can say which part comes out of a seed first: the root.
By the end I can say what the root does and what the shoot does.
By the end I can plant a seed, look after the seed, and say what I saw each day.
By the end I can say that a seed grows into the same kind of plant as the plant that made the seed.

terms.meaning: A seed is a tiny living plant packed with food, inside a hard coat.
terms.example: Chana, rajma, moong and the black seeds in a papaya are all seeds.
terms.art: A row of seeds on a steel plate: chana, rajma, moong, a mango stone and black papaya seeds.

terms.meaning: To sprout is to start growing. A sprout is also the young plant that comes out of a seed.
terms.example: Moong soaked overnight and kept on a wet cloth sprout in a day.
terms.art: A handful of moong seeds, each with a little white tail coming out.

terms.meaning: The root is the part of a plant that grows down into the soil. A root drinks water and holds the plant in place.
terms.example: Pull up a weed gently, and the thin white threads at the bottom are the roots.
terms.art: A small plant lifted out of the soil, showing white roots at the bottom.

terms.meaning: The shoot is the part of a plant that grows up into the light. The stem and leaves grow from the shoot.
terms.example: A new chana plant pushes a curled green shoot up out of the soil.
terms.art: A curled green shoot pushing up through soil, like a bent finger.

terms.meaning: Seed leaves are the first leaves that open on a young plant. They often look different from the plant's later leaves.
terms.example: A young pumpkin plant opens two round, smooth seed leaves first.
terms.art: A young pumpkin seedling with two round seed leaves and a tiny new leaf in the middle.

explanations.concept: A seed is a tiny living plant
explanations.context: This card says what is inside a seed.
explanations.definition: A seed holds a tiny baby plant and a store of food, wrapped in a seed coat.
explanations.description: A seed looks like a small stone, but the seed is alive. Inside the hard coat there is a tiny baby plant, with a store of food next to the baby plant. A dry seed waits, sometimes for years. When the seed gets water, the seed swells and starts to grow.
examples: A dry chana seed in a jar stays the same for months. Soaked overnight, the chana is fat and soft by morning.
Rice, wheat, chana and dal are seeds that people eat.
A mango stone has the mango tree's seed inside.
explanations.art: A big drawing of a chana seed opened up, with the seed coat, a tiny baby plant at one edge, and the two big halves full of food.

explanations.context: Remember the chana you dug up each day? This card says what you saw.
explanations.definition: When a seed sprouts, the root nearly always comes out first and grows down. The shoot comes later and grows up.
explanations.description: The root comes out first, through the seed coat. The root grows down into the soil, drinks water and holds the plant in place. Then the shoot grows up, curled like a bent finger so the soil does not scrape the tender tip. So for the first days, most of the growing happens under the soil, where we cannot see it.
examples: Your chana grew a white root before any green showed above the soil.
Moong sprouts in the kitchen have a white tail. That tail is the root.
A young peepal plant growing out of a wall crack sends roots deep into the crack.
explanations.art: Four chana seeds in a row on a plate, from left to right: a fat seed, a seed with a short root, a seed with a long root, and a seed with a long root and a curled shoot.

explanations.concept: A seed grows into the same kind of plant as the plant that made the seed
explanations.context: This card is about why a mango seed never grows into a coconut palm.
explanations.definition: A seed grows into the same kind of plant as the plant that made the seed.
explanations.description: Plant a pumpkin seed, and you get a pumpkin plant. Plant a chana seed, and you get a chana plant. The size of the seed does not decide the plant. The kind of seed does.
examples: Seeds from a pumpkin grow into pumpkin plants.
A tamarind seed grows into a tamarind tree.
A mango stone grows into a mango tree, never a coconut palm.
explanations.art: Three pairs side by side: a pumpkin seed and a pumpkin plant, a tamarind seed and a tamarind tree, and a mango stone and a mango tree.

agreed.text: Seeds are alive. Each seed holds a tiny baby plant.
agreed.evidence: Open a soaked chana or rajma and you can see the baby plant at one edge. Dry seeds kept for months still sprout when they get water.

agreed.text: Seeds need water to start growing.
agreed.evidence: Dry seeds in a jar never sprout. The same seeds sprout within a few days once they are kept damp.

agreed.text: In almost all seeds, the root comes out first.
agreed.evidence: People who study seeds watch thousands of them sprout. The root comes out first and grows down. Scientists even use the root coming out as the sign that a seed has sprouted.

challenging.claim: Seeds are not alive. They are like little stones.
challenging.who: A very common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake: that seeds are not alive.
challenging.for: A dry seed does not move, eat or grow. A dry seed looks and feels like a small stone.
challenging.against: A pebble in damp soil stays a pebble. A seed in damp soil swells, grows a root and becomes a plant. Seeds are alive, and they wait until they get water.

challenging.claim: A big seed grows into a big plant.
challenging.context: This card is about a common guess: that big seeds make big plants.
challenging.for: Some big seeds, like a coconut, do grow into tall plants.
challenging.against: A banyan seed is tiny, smaller than a grain of rai, and a banyan becomes a huge tree. A rajma seed is big, and a rajma plant stays small. The kind of seed decides, not the size.

challenging.claim: Leaves grow first, and roots come later.
challenging.who: A common guess, because leaves are what we see first
challenging.context: This card is about a common guess: that leaves come before roots.
challenging.for: When we plant a seed, the first thing we see is a green shoot coming up.
challenging.against: Under the soil, the root came out days before. Dig up a sprouting chana and you see a long root and no leaves yet.

big_questions.q: For days, nothing showed above the soil. But the seed was busy. What else might be busy where we cannot see?
big_questions.hint: Think about your own body, the ground under a building, and the sky at night.

big_questions.q: How does a root know which way is down, in the dark under the soil?
big_questions.hint: You know which way is down even with your eyes shut. How do you know?

big_questions.q: A dry seed can wait in a jar for a year. Is a seed in a jar asleep, or awake and waiting?
big_questions.hint: What wakes you up in the morning? What wakes a seed?

big_questions.q: Every tree you know started as one small seed. Where did all the wood come from?
big_questions.hint: The seed was tiny. Think about what the plant took in, every day, for years.

story.title: The Tree on the Terrace Wall
story.note: Leela, Varun and Paati are made up. Peepal and banyan plants really do sprout from cracks in walls in Indian cities, from seeds dropped by birds, and their roots grow deep into the cracks.
text: Leela lived in a flat in Chennai, at the top of an old building. She was six. Her little brother Varun was four. Every evening, they went up to the terrace with their grandmother, Paati, to take the dry clothes off the line.

One evening, Leela saw something green on the wall of the water tank. A tiny plant was growing out of a crack in the cement. The plant had three small leaves. Each leaf was shaped like a heart, with a long pointed tip.
'Paati, look! Who planted a plant up here?' asked Leela.
Paati bent down and looked. 'Nobody planted this one,' she said. 'This is a peepal. A peepal grows into a very big tree.'
Varun laughed. 'A big tree? That's tiny! And there's no soil here. Only a wall.'

Paati pointed to the old peepal tree down on the road. The tree's branches were full of small round figs. Crows and koels sat in the branches, eating them. 'Every fig is full of tiny seeds,' said Paati. 'The birds eat the figs. Then they fly away and leave droppings, and the seeds come out in the droppings. One seed fell into this crack. The rain came. And the seed began to grow.'
Leela looked at the tiny plant again. 'How can such a little seed hold on to a wall?' she asked.
'Let's look,' said Paati. She took a hairpin out of her bun. Very gently, she scraped away some of the loose dust from the crack. Leela and Varun leaned in close.
Down in the crack, there was a thin white root. The root went down and down, much further than the plant was tall. Then the root turned a corner and went deeper still.
'The root is longer than the whole plant!' said Leela.

'Yes,' said Paati. 'When a seed wakes up, the root comes out first. The root finds water and holds on tight. Only then does the shoot grow up into the light. So most of this little peepal is hidden inside the wall.'
Varun was quiet for a moment. Then he said, 'If the root keeps going, will the wall crack?'
'It might,' said Paati. 'Peepal roots are strong. In a few years, a peepal root can split a wall.'
Leela did not want the peepal to break their tank. But she did not want to pull out the little plant either. 'Can we move the peepal to a pot?' she asked.

So the next morning, they filled an old paint tin with soil. Paati worked the little plant out of the crack, very slowly, so the long root came out whole. Leela held the pot, and Varun poured water from a steel tumbler.
Every evening after that, Leela checked the peepal. For a week, nothing changed on top. 'Is she sad?' asked Varun.
'She is busy underneath,' said Leela. 'The root comes first. You'll see.'
On the ninth day, a new red leaf unrolled at the top. Varun ran to tell Paati. 'The peepal is growing up now!' he shouted.
story.epiphany: Leela sees that the little peepal's root is much longer than the plant above, and understands that a seed grows down first, to find water and hold on, before the shoot grows up.
ask: Who planted the peepal on the terrace wall?
Why was the root longer than the plant?
For a week, nothing changed on top of the pot. What do you think the peepal was doing?
art: A girl, a small boy and their grandmother on a city terrace with washing on a line, looking at a tiny heart-leafed plant growing out of a crack in a water tank wall.
A grandmother gently scraping a wall crack with a hairpin, showing a long thin white root going deep into the crack.
A girl holding an old paint tin that holds a small peepal plant, and a boy pouring water from a steel tumbler.

games.title: Whose Seed? A memory game
games.players: 2 to 4 players. Anyone who cannot read yet asks another player to read the card.
games.context: This is a memory game. Half the cards are seeds and half are the plants they grow into. Players match each seed to the plant that grows from the seed.

printables.title: 16 cards to cut out. Each card has its name on it.

rules: Cut out the 16 cards. Colour the border of each card: brown for seeds and green for plants.
Mix the cards and lay them face down in rows.
On your turn, turn over one brown card and one green card. Read them out loud.
If the seed grows into that plant, keep the pair and have another turn.
If not, turn both cards back over. The next player has a turn.

When all the pairs are found, each player counts their pairs. The player with the most pairs wins, or everyone wins together if it is a tie. Then lay the pairs out and look: which tiny seed made the biggest plant?

setup.art: Sixteen small cards with names on them lying on a floor mat, half with brown borders and half with green borders.
setup.caption: 1. Colour the borders brown and green. Lay the cards face down.

setup.art: A child turning over a card with a mango stone and a card with a mango tree, smiling.
setup.caption: 2. Turn one seed card and one plant card. Is it a pair?

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Colour the borders: brown for seeds, green for plants. 3. Mix the cards and lay them face down.
flow.say: Each brown card is a seed. Each green card is a plant. Can you find each seed and their own plant?
flow.kid: Brown cards are seeds. Green cards are plants. Find the pairs.

flow.do: Take turns. Each player turns one brown and one green card. Read both out loud.
flow.say: What did you turn over? Does this seed grow into this plant? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Turn one brown card and one green card. Do they go together?

ask.q: Can a mango stone grow into a coconut palm?
good: No. A mango seed grows into a mango tree.
Each seed grows into their own kind.

flow.parent: Let the child say why before you check. If they are unsure, ask what fruit the seed came from.

flow.do: Lay out all the pairs. Count each player's pairs. Look at the banyan pair.
flow.say: Look at the banyan seed and the banyan tree. Which seed is smallest? Which plant is biggest?
flow.kid: Look at the tiny banyan seed. Look at the huge banyan tree. Are they a pair?

check.q: A banyan seed is tiny. What does a banyan seed grow into?
check.why: A banyan seed is smaller than a grain of rai, but a banyan grows into a huge tree. The kind of seed decides, not the size.

flow.parent: The banyan pair is the surprise. Banyan seeds are tiny, about a millimetre across.

games.title: Root Down, Shoot Up: a moving game
games.players: 1 or more players and a caller
games.context: This is a moving game about how a seed sprouts. The caller reads a card, and the players move the way that part of the plant grows.

items.b: Curl up small and keep still. A dry seed waits.
Puff out your cheeks and stretch a little. The seed soaks up water and swells.
Push one foot down and out. The root comes out first and grows down.
Make a slurping sound. The root drinks water from the soil.
Press both feet hard into the floor. The root holds the plant in place.
Bend your back and push up slowly, head down, like a bent finger. The shoot comes up curled.
Straighten up and lift your head. The shoot reaches the light.
Open both hands wide above your head. The seed leaves open.
Droop down slowly. A young plant with no water wilts.
Stand up tall again. A drink helps the young plant stand up.

rules: The caller puts the ten cards in the order they are printed, with Dry seed on top.
The caller reads the front of the top card out loud.
Everyone moves the way the back of the card says. The caller reads the back if needed.
After a few cards, the caller says 'Freeze!' Everyone stays still. The caller asks one player what their body is doing, and which part of the plant does that.
Swap callers after all ten cards, and play again. This time the players say what comes next before the caller reads the card.

setup.art: A child curled up small on the floor like a seed, with a grown-up holding a card.
setup.caption: 1. Start curled up, like a dry seed.

setup.art: The same child pressing their feet into the floor with arms stretched up and hands open wide.
setup.caption: 2. Root down, shoot up, leaves open.

flow.do: Clear a space on the floor. Put the cards in order, with the Dry seed card on top.
flow.say: You are a seed. Curl up small. I will read a card, and you move.
flow.kid: Curl up small. You are a dry seed.

flow.do: Read the cards one at a time. Do the moves together the first time.
flow.say: Root! Which way does the root grow? Show me with your feet.
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Move like that part of the plant.
flow.parent: If the child shoots up before the root, say 'Root first!' and let them try again.

flow.do: Say Freeze. Ask what each player is.
flow.say: Freeze! What is your body doing? Which part of the plant does that? What is that part doing for the plant?
flow.kid: Freeze! What is your body doing? Which part of the plant does that?

check.q: What does the root do for a young plant?
check.why: The root grows down into the soil. The root drinks water and holds the plant in place.

experiments.title: Peek Under the Soil: what does a seed do first?
experiments.context: In this experiment you plant five chana seeds in a box of soil. Each day you gently dig one up, look at the seed, and put the seed back. You find out what a seed does under the soil before you can see anything.
experiments.question: After we plant a seed, what happens under the soil before anything shows on top?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Under the soil, what will the seed grow first: a root, a leaf, or nothing yet? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All five seeds come from one packet, are soaked together, and are planted in the same soil at the same depth. The only difference is how many days each seed has had in the soil.

materials.item: whole chana seeds, kala chana or white chana, from the kitchen
a bowl of water for soaking
a small plastic box, a cut-off milk packet or a pot, with a few holes poked in the bottom, on a plate or tray
soil from a pot plant, or a small bag of potting soil
5 toothpicks or ice-cream sticks, numbered 1 to 5
a spoon, a plate and a damp cloth

schedule.what: In the evening, soak 6 chana seeds in a bowl of water.
Plant 5 seeds, each next to a numbered stick. Guess what will happen.
Dig up seed 1. Look, draw, and put the seed back.
Dig up seed 2. Look, draw, and put the seed back.
Dig up seed 3. Look, draw, and put the seed back.
Dig up seed 4. Look at seed 5 from the top. Put all your drawings in a row.
Look for seed 5's shoot coming up. If it is not up, look again each day.

experiments.record: Each day, draw the seed you dug up, as big as your hand. On day 5, put the drawings in a row.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results. Your seeds may be a day faster or slower.
rows: Fat and soft. A tiny white tip poking out.
A white root as long as a fingernail, going down.
A long root with little side roots. A curled shoot starting.
A long root. A curled shoot, growing up.
A green shoot, or a small bump, showing above the soil.

setup.art: Five soaked chana seeds being pushed into a box of soil, each next to a numbered ice-cream stick.
setup.caption: 1. Plant five soaked seeds, each next to a numbered stick.

setup.art: A child's fingers gently lifting soil with a spoon next to stick number 2, showing a chana seed with a short white root.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, dig up one seed gently with a spoon.

setup.art: Four drawings in a row on a table: a fat seed, a seed with a short root, a seed with a long root, and a seed with a long root and a curled shoot.
setup.caption: 3. Draw each seed. Put the drawings in a row.

flow.do: In the evening, put 6 whole chana seeds in a bowl. Cover them with water.
flow.say: We are going to plant chana seeds tomorrow. Tonight they soak in water. Feel how hard they are now.
flow.kid: Feel the hard chana. Put them in the water. They soak all night.
flow.parent: Use whole chana, not dal. Split dal is damaged where the baby plant sits, so dal does not sprout.

flow.do: 1. Fill the box with soil, 3 fingers deep. 2. Push 5 sticks into the soil, in a row, a hand apart. 3. Next to each stick, push one seed down one finger-joint deep. 4. Cover with soil. 5. Sprinkle water until the soil is damp. 6. Put the box by a bright window, out of hot afternoon sun.
flow.say: Feel the chana now. What has changed since last night? Now let's plant each seed next to a stick.
flow.kid: Feel the chana. Are they hard or soft? Plant one seed next to each stick.

ask.q: What changed after the night in water?
good: They got bigger.
They are soft now.
They drank the water.

flow.parent: The sticks tell you where each seed is, so you can dig up the right one. Keep the spare seed in the bowl to compare.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess, and to say why. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Tomorrow we dig up seed 1. What will the seed have done under the soil? A root, a leaf, or nothing yet? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Under the soil, what will the seed grow first? Why?

good: Nothing, because the soil is dark.
A leaf, because plants have leaves.
A root, because roots go in the soil.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Many children guess that a leaf comes first, or that nothing happens in the dark. Don't tell them what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Next to stick 1, lift the soil gently with a spoon. 2. Lay seed 1 on the damp cloth. 3. Look closely and draw. 4. Put the seed back in the hole, cover the seed with soil and water a little.
flow.say: Let's dig up seed 1 very gently. What do you see? Is anything coming out?
flow.kid: Dig up seed 1 gently. Look closely. What is coming out?

good: Fat and soft.
The skin is cracking.
A tiny white tip is coming out.

flow.parent: Handle the seed by the sides, not the white tip. Put the seed back quickly, root down. Most replanted seeds keep growing.

flow.do: On day 3, dig up seed 2 the same way. Draw it and put the drawing next to yesterday's drawing.
flow.say: Here is seed 2. Which way is the white part growing? Up or down?
flow.kid: Dig up seed 2. Which way is the white part going?

good: The root.
The root, going down.

flow.parent: On day 3 the root is usually as long as a fingernail. In a cold room it may be a day slower.

flow.do: Dig up seed 3 the same way. Put the drawing next to the others.
flow.say: Here is seed 3. Is the root longer than yesterday? Is anything else coming out?
flow.kid: Dig up seed 3. Is the root longer? What else is coming out?

good: The root is longer.
There are little side roots.
A curled shoot is starting.

flow.parent: Seed 3 usually has a long root, often with little side roots.

flow.do: On day 4, dig up seed 3 the same way. Draw it and put the drawing in the row.
flow.say: Here is seed 3. Is the root longer than yesterday? Is anything new coming out?
flow.kid: Dig up seed 3. Is the root longer? Is anything new coming out?
flow.parent: On day 4 the root is usually long, with little side roots, and a curled shoot may be starting. Everything may be a day slower in a cold room.

flow.do: 1. On day 5, dig up seed 4. 2. Look at the top of the soil by stick 5. 3. Put all four drawings in a row, from seed 1 to seed 4.
flow.say: Seed 5 is coming up now. But was the seed doing nothing before today? What did you find out?
flow.kid: Look at all your drawings. What came out first? What came next?

ask.q: What came out first, the root or the shoot?
good: The root came first.
The root, then the shoot.

ask.q: Above the soil, what could we see?
good: Nothing, or only a tiny bump.
Nothing, but underneath there was a long root.

check.q: Under the soil, what did the chana seed grow first?
check.why: A seed grows a root first. The root grows down, drinks water and holds on. The shoot comes later.

flow.parent: Ask for the claim (the root comes first), the evidence (the four drawings) and the reason (the root needs to drink and hold on). Chana can need 6 to 10 days to show above the soil, so if seed 5 is not up, wait a few more days.

flow.do: On day 6, look at the top of the soil by stick 5 for a green shoot. If it is not up yet, look again each day. Ask your child to say what they found out.
flow.say: Look at seed 5. Is a green shoot up yet? For days nothing showed on top, but was the seed doing nothing? What did you find out?
flow.kid: Look at seed 5. Was the seed busy before we saw anything? Say what you found.

good: The root comes first, under the soil.
The seed was growing before we could see anything.
First the root goes down, then the shoot comes up.

flow.parent: Ask for the claim (the root comes first), the evidence (the four drawings) and the reason (the root needs to drink and hold on). Chana can take 6 to 10 days to show above the soil, so wait a few days if seed 5 is not up.

experiments.title: Big Seed, Small Seed: who sprouts first?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put rajma, moong and rai seeds on wet tissue, side by side. You watch to find out which kind shows a root first.
experiments.question: Does a big seed sprout faster than a small seed?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which seed will show a root first: the big rajma, the middle moong, or the tiny rai? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three kinds soak for the same time, sit on the same wet tissue on one plate, and get the same water in the same place. Only the kind of seed is different.

materials.item: 6 rajma, 6 moong and 6 rai (mustard) seeds from the kitchen
3 small bowls for soaking
a steel plate with 2 layers of kitchen tissue or an old cotton hanky
a spoon and a cup of water
a tea strainer

schedule.what: In the evening, soak each kind of seed in a separate bowl.
Lay the seeds on wet tissue in three rows. Guess which will show a root first.
Look at each row. Count the seeds with a root. Wet the tissue.
Look again. Which row won? Do all three grow the root first?

experiments.record: Each day, put a tick next to every seed that has a root.

setup.art: Three small bowls with rajma, moong and tiny round rai seeds soaking in water.
setup.caption: 1. Soak each kind overnight.

setup.art: A steel plate with wet tissue and three rows of seeds: big rajma, green moong and tiny rai, a few with white tails.
setup.caption: 2. Lay them in three rows on wet tissue. Watch for roots.

flow.do: In the evening, put 6 rajma, 6 moong and 6 rai in three small bowls. Cover each with water.
flow.say: Look at the three kinds of seed. Which is the biggest? Which is the smallest?
flow.kid: Look at the three seeds. Which is biggest? Which is smallest?
flow.parent: Do not eat these seeds raw: raw rajma is poisonous. Small seeds must stay out of mouths and noses, so keep the plate away from small children. Soaked rai goes slimy. That is normal.

flow.do: 1. Wet the tissue on the plate. 2. Pour each bowl through a tea strainer to drain the seeds. 3. Lay them in three rows. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Which seed will show a root first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put the seeds in three rows. Which will show a root first? Why?

good: The rajma, because rajma are biggest and strongest.
The rai, because they are small and quick.

flow.parent: Many children guess the big rajma, because big seems strong. Don't say what will happen. Keep the tissue wet, with no puddle.

flow.do: Look at each row. Count the seeds with a white root. Sprinkle water on the tissue.
flow.say: Count the seeds with a root in each row. Which row has the most?
flow.kid: Count the seeds with a white root in each row.
flow.parent: Moong and rai usually show roots first, often within a day. Rajma are usually a day or two slower. If rajma win in your home, that is a real result too.

flow.do: Look again. Talk about who was first, and what came out first on every seed.
flow.say: Who was first? Did the big seed sprout faster? And on every seed, what came out first?
flow.kid: Who was first? On every seed, what came out first?

ask.q: Did the biggest seed sprout first?
good: No, the small ones were faster.
No, the rajma was slow.

flow.parent: A big seed takes longer to soak up enough water, which is probably part of why rajma are slower. The kind of seed matters too.

activities.title: The Seed Feely Bag
activities.context: In this activity you put kitchen seeds in a cloth bag. You feel one seed at a time without looking, and guess which kind of seed you are holding.

materials.item: a cloth bag, a clean sock or a pillow cover
whole seeds: rajma, chana, groundnut, moong, and a tamarind seed or a mango stone if you have one
a steel plate

schedule.what: Feel the seeds without looking. Guess each one.

activities.record: Draw the seed that was hardest to guess.

setup.art: A steel plate with rajma, chana, groundnuts, moong and a tamarind seed, and a cloth bag next to the plate.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the seeds on the plate first.

setup.art: A child with a hand inside a cloth bag, eyes closed, feeling a seed.
setup.caption: 2. Feel one seed in the bag. Guess which it is.

flow.do: Put two of each seed on the plate. Let your child look at and touch each one.
flow.say: These are all seeds. Each one has a tiny baby plant inside. Feel each kind. Which is smooth? Which is wrinkly?
flow.kid: These are all seeds. Touch each one. Which is smooth? Which is wrinkly?
flow.parent: Chana is wrinkly, rajma is smooth and shiny, groundnut has a thin papery skin, moong is small and smooth.

flow.do: Put one of each seed in the bag. Your child reaches in, picks one, feels the seed and guesses, then pulls the seed out to check.
flow.say: Pick one seed. Don't look. Is the seed big or small, smooth or wrinkly? Which kind of seed are you holding?
flow.kid: Feel one seed without looking. Guess which kind of seed. Then look.

good: Wrinkly, so chana.
Big and smooth, so rajma.

flow.parent: Small seeds can choke a young child. Stay beside your child, and keep the seeds out of mouths and noses.

flow.do: Ask your child what would grow if each seed were planted.
flow.say: All of these are seeds. What would happen if we planted each one?
flow.kid: What would grow from each seed?

ask.q: What would grow from the groundnut?
good: A groundnut plant.
A new groundnut plant, the same kind as the plant the seed came from.

flow.parent: Raw groundnuts sprout. Roasted ones do not, because heat kills the baby plant inside.

activities.title: Line Up the Seeds: smallest to biggest
activities.context: In this activity you put seeds in a line from the smallest to the biggest. Then you talk about which plant each one grows into.

materials.item: a few of each seed: rai, moong, chana, rajma, groundnut, and a mango stone or a tamarind seed if you have one
a strip of paper and a crayon

schedule.what: Line up the seeds by size. Talk about the plants they grow into.

activities.record: Draw your line of seeds on the paper strip, smallest at one end.

setup.art: A paper strip on the floor with seeds in a line: tiny rai, moong, chana, rajma, a groundnut and a big mango stone.
setup.caption: 1. Put the seeds in a line, smallest to biggest.

setup.art: A child pointing at the tiny rai at one end and the big mango stone at the other.
setup.caption: 2. Point to the smallest seed and the biggest seed.

flow.do: Mix the seeds on the floor. Your child lines them up on the strip, smallest to biggest.
flow.say: Can you put these seeds in a line, from the smallest to the biggest?
flow.kid: Put the seeds in a line. Smallest first. Biggest last.
flow.parent: Rai is smallest, then moong, then chana. Rajma and groundnut are close in size, so either order is fine. A mango stone is the biggest.

flow.do: Talk about the plant each seed grows into.
flow.say: A mango stone grows into a big tree. A rajma grows into a small plant. A banyan seed is even smaller than rai, and a banyan grows into a huge tree. Does a bigger seed always make a bigger plant?
flow.kid: Does a big seed always grow a big plant? What about the tiny banyan seed?

ask.q: Does a big seed always make a big plant?
good: No. The banyan seed is tiny and the tree is huge.
No. It depends on the kind of seed.

activities.title: What's in the Pumpkin? Save seeds to plant
activities.context: In this activity you take the seeds out of a pumpkin, a melon or a watermelon from the kitchen. You wash and count some, and keep the best ones to plant.

materials.item: the seeds scooped out of a pumpkin, an ash gourd, a muskmelon or a watermelon, on cooking day
a sieve or a steel plate, and water
a newspaper to dry them on

schedule.what: Wash the seeds. Count ten. Spread them to dry for two days.

activities.record: Draw one seed and the fruit they came from.

setup.art: A cut pumpkin with seeds being scooped into a steel sieve.
setup.caption: 1. Scoop the seeds into a sieve and wash them.

setup.art: Flat pale pumpkin seeds drying on a newspaper by a window.
setup.caption: 2. Spread the seeds on newspaper to dry.

flow.do: When you cook a pumpkin or cut a melon, scoop the seeds into a sieve. Your child washes off the stringy bits under the tap.
flow.say: Look how many seeds were inside one pumpkin. Each seed holds a tiny baby pumpkin plant.
flow.kid: Wash the seeds. Rub off the stringy bits.
flow.parent: A grown-up cuts the fruit. The child only scoops and washes.

flow.do: Count ten seeds out loud together, into a line.
flow.say: Let's count ten seeds. If all ten grew, how many pumpkin plants would we have?
flow.kid: Count ten seeds. Put them in a line.

ask.q: What will grow from a pumpkin seed?
good: A pumpkin plant.
A new pumpkin plant.

flow.do: Spread the seeds on newspaper to dry for two days. Keep some for the project 'Plant a Seed from Your Plate'.
flow.say: We'll dry these and plant some. Which plant will come up?
flow.kid: Spread the seeds out to dry. Soon we will plant them.
flow.parent: Fresh seeds can also be planted straight away. Seeds from a store-bought pumpkin or melon usually sprout well.

projects.title: Plant a Seed from Your Plate
projects.context: In this two-week project you plant seeds from a fruit or vegetable you ate, in a cup of soil. You look after them and watch a new plant grow.

materials.item: 4 seeds from a pumpkin, a melon, a watermelon or a tomato
a paper cup or a cut-off plastic bottle with 3 small holes poked in the bottom
soil from a pot plant, or a small bag of potting soil
a saucer under the cup, and a spoon for watering

schedule.what: Fill the cup with soil. Plant 4 seeds, one finger-joint deep. Water. Give each plant a name.
Touch the soil. If dry, sprinkle water. Look for any change.
Look for curled shoots coming up. Draw the cup.
Look at the seed leaves. Is a tiny new leaf in the middle yet? Is it the same shape?
Draw your plants. Compare the seed leaves with the newer leaves. Tell someone at home the story of your seed, from plate to plant.

projects.record: Draw your cup on day 1, day 6 and day 14.

setup.art: A child pushing pale pumpkin seeds into a paper cup of soil on a saucer.
setup.caption: 1. Plant 4 seeds, one finger-joint deep.

setup.art: The same paper cup on a windowsill with two young pumpkin plants, each with two round seed leaves.
setup.caption: 2. Water a little. Watch the shoots come up.

flow.do: 1. Fill the cup with soil. 2. Push 4 seeds in, one finger-joint deep, flat side down. 3. Cover and sprinkle water until the soil is damp. 4. Put the cup on a saucer by a bright window.
flow.say: These seeds came from our pumpkin. Let's plant them. What do you think will grow? What name shall we give each plant?
flow.kid: Push 4 seeds into the soil. Cover them. Sprinkle water. Give each plant a name.
flow.parent: Poke holes in the bottom so extra water drains out. Soggy soil makes seeds rot.

flow.do: Every two or three days, touch the soil. If the top feels dry, sprinkle 3 spoons of water.
flow.say: Touch the soil. Is the soil dry or damp? Does your seed need a drink?
flow.kid: Touch the soil. Dry? Give some water. Damp? Leave it.
flow.wait: Check every two or three days.

flow.do: Look for curled shoots coming up. Draw the cup.
flow.say: Look! What is coming up? Why do you think the shoot is curled over?
flow.kid: Look for a curled shoot. Draw what you see.
flow.parent: Pumpkin and melon seeds usually come up in 4 to 8 days in warm weather. Tomato seeds can take up to 2 weeks. In a cold room, they take longer.

flow.do: Look at the seed leaves. Look for a tiny new leaf in the middle, if it has come yet.
flow.say: Look at the first two leaves, the seed leaves. Is a tiny new leaf in the middle yet? If so, is it the same shape?
flow.kid: Look at the first two leaves. Draw one.
flow.parent: Pumpkin seed leaves are smooth and round. The true leaves come a little later and are big, rough and wavy at the edges. If you cannot see one yet, look again on day 14.

flow.do: Your child draws the plants and compares the seed leaves with the newer leaves. Then your child tells someone at home the story, from plate to plant.
flow.say: Tell your story. Where did the seed come from? What came out first? What happened next? Are the newer leaves the same shape as the seed leaves?
flow.kid: Tell someone at home the story of your seed. Where did the seed come from? What grew first?

ask.q: What kind of plant grew from the pumpkin seed?
good: A pumpkin plant.
The same kind as the plant the seed came from.

flow.parent: If you have a balcony or a big pot, move one plant to a bigger pot. Pumpkin plants climb and spread, and need space.

challenges.title: Water While We Sleep
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. Seeds on tissue dry out if nobody waters them. Can you keep them wet for three days without pouring any water?
challenges.problem: Your family is going away for three days. You want your moong seeds to keep sprouting. Make something that keeps the tissue wet, with nobody pouring water.
constraints: Nobody adds water for three days.
The seeds must not sit under water.
materials: kitchen tissue or a cotton hanky
a strip of old cotton cloth
general: Stand a cotton strip in a tumbler of water and lay the other end under the tissue. The cloth draws water up.
Put the seeds on wet tissue in a box with a loosely closed lid, so the water does not dry away.
creative: Put a wet sponge under the tissue, like a water tank.
Cut a plastic bottle in half. Turn the top half upside down into the bottom half, with a cloth strip going down into the water.
Cover the plate loosely with a clear plastic bag. The water that dries off the tissue collects on the bag and drips back.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Draw it, make it, and test it for three days. Did the tissue stay wet? Did the seeds sprout?

setup.art: A steel tumbler of water with a strip of cotton cloth hanging over the rim and lying under a wet tissue with moong seeds on a plate.
setup.caption: 1. A cloth strip goes from the water to the tissue.

setup.art: The same set-up three days later, with the moong showing long white roots and the tissue still damp.
setup.caption: 2. Three days later: is the tissue still wet?

flow.do: Show a dry tissue and a wet tissue. Leave a wet tissue on a plate and come back in the evening.
flow.say: If nobody waters the seeds, what happens to the tissue? How could we keep the tissue wet without pouring water?
flow.kid: What happens to wet tissue if nobody waters it? How could we keep it wet?
flow.parent: On a warm day, a thin wet tissue can dry in a few hours. For step 2, soak a handful of moong the evening before.

flow.do: Your child picks an idea, or invents one, and builds it with your help, using the moong soaked the night before.
flow.say: Which idea will you try? Why do you think it will keep the tissue wet?
flow.kid: Pick an idea. Build it. Say why you think it will work.

good: The cloth drinks the water and takes it to the tissue.
The lid stops the water drying away.

flow.parent: A grown-up cuts any plastic bottle. Do not eat these sprouts. They are for looking.

flow.do: Check once a day for three days. Do not add water. Look at the seeds and touch the tissue.
flow.say: Is the tissue still damp? Are the seeds sprouting? What came out of them first?
flow.kid: Touch the tissue. Is the tissue wet? Look at the seeds. What came out first?

check.q: A cotton strip stands in water and touches the tissue. What does the strip do?
options: Carries water up to the tissue
check.why: Water creeps along cotton threads. The strip carries water from the tumbler to the tissue, so the seeds stay damp.

flow.wait: Check every day for three days.

items.p: Remember the chana you dug up each day? What came out of the seed first?
items.why: The root comes out first and grows down. The shoot comes later.

items.p: Draw a chana seed under the soil on day 4. Show what is growing out of the seed.
items.a: A seed with a long white root going down, and maybe a small curled shoot.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the root going down and longer than the shoot, all under the soil.
items.art: An empty box of soil drawn from the side, with a line for the top of the soil.

items.p: Draw a line from each seed to the plant they grow into.
items.why: Each seed grows into the same kind of plant as the plant the seed came from.
items.art: A mango stone, a pumpkin seed and a coconut on one side, and a mango tree, a pumpkin plant and a coconut palm on the other.

items.p: A dry seed is not alive.
items.why: False. A dry seed is alive and waiting. Give the seed water, and the seed grows.

items.p: Colour the root brown and the shoot green.
items.a: The white part going down is the root. The curled part going up is the shoot.
items.why: The root grows down to drink and hold on. The shoot grows up into the light.
items.art: A large drawing of a sprouting chana with a root going down and a curled shoot going up, both uncoloured.

items.p: Put the pictures in order, from first to last.
items: A shoot comes up out of the soil
a: A shoot comes up out of the soil
items.why: First the seed drinks water and swells. Then the root comes out. Then the shoot grows up.
items.art: Four small pictures in a mixed-up order: a shoot above the soil, a dry seed, a seed with a root, and a fat soaked seed.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: feel a dry chana and a soaked chana. How are they different? Why?
items.a: The soaked chana is fat and soft. It drank water. The dry chana is hard and small.
items.why: A strong answer says what the child felt and says that the seed took in water.

items.p: Which one is NOT a seed?
items.why: A pebble is a small stone. Planted in damp soil, a pebble stays a pebble. The others are seeds and can grow.

items.p: Thenmozhi, a girl in Madurai, plants a chana seed in dry soil and never waters the seed. What happens?
opts: The seed turns into a pebble
items.why: A seed needs water to start growing. In dry soil the seed waits and does not grow.

items.p: Two friends in Guwahati look at a pot where they planted seeds three days ago. Nothing shows on top.

views.says: Nothing is happening. The seeds are dead. Let's throw the soil away.
The seeds might be growing roots underneath. Let's wait.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Say what you saw in your own pot. Then say one thing the other friend got right.
items.a: Moni, because our chana grew roots under the soil for days before anything showed. Bornali is right that a seed can die, for example if the soil stays too wet.
items.why: A strong answer uses the dug-up seeds as evidence, and fairly says that sometimes a seed does not grow.

items.p: Count the seeds in the picture that have a root. How many have no root yet?
items.a: 4 seeds have a root. 2 have no root yet.
items.why: Seeds sprout at different times. 6 seeds take away 4 with roots leaves 2.
items.art: A plate of 6 moong seeds: 4 with white tails and 2 without.

items.p: Remember when you put rajma, moong and rai on wet tissue? Which usually showed a root first?
items.why: Small seeds like moong and rai usually sprout first. A big seed usually takes longer to soak up enough water.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: why do you think the root comes out before the shoot?
items.a: The root has to drink water and hold the seed in place before the shoot can grow up.
items.why: A strong answer gives a job of the root: drinking water, or holding on.

items.p: Draw a young plant. Show the root and the shoot, with an arrow for the way each one grows.
items.a: The root with an arrow pointing down, the shoot with an arrow pointing up.
items.why: Roots grow down into the soil and shoots grow up into the light.

items.p: Split dal can sprout, just like whole moong.
items.why: False. Splitting the seed damages the baby plant's root tip, so split dal does not sprout. Whole, raw seeds can.

items.p: Sort these: will they sprout, or not?
items.why: Whole, raw seeds have a living baby plant inside. Roasting kills the baby plant, and splitting breaks off the root tip. A marble was never alive.

items.p: Write these words next to the right part of the young pumpkin plant: root, shoot, seed leaves.
items.a: Root at the bottom in the soil, shoot as the stem, seed leaves as the two round leaves at the top.
items.why: The seed leaves are the first leaves to open. They look different from the later leaves.
items.art: A young pumpkin plant in a cup, with the soil cut away to show the root, and three empty label lines.

items.p: Anjali in Surat wants to grow a tamarind tree. She has a tamarind seed and a pumpkin seed. Which one should she plant? Why?
items.a: The tamarind seed, because a seed grows into the same kind of plant the seed came from.
items.why: A strong answer says each seed grows into their own kind.

items.p: Put these in order: the story of a seed from your plate.
items.why: The seeds come from the fruit. After planting, the root grows first, then the shoot.

items.p: Draw a line from each part to the job it does.
items.why: Each part has a job. The seed coat protects the seed while the seed waits.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: many people think a seed needs sunlight to start growing. How could you test this with two cups of damp soil and some chana?
items.a: Plant soaked chana in two cups. Keep one cup in the light and one in a dark cupboard. Give both the same water. See which seeds grow a root.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the light and keeps the seeds, soil and water the same.

videos.title: Bean time-lapse in soil, seen from the side
videos.why: Shows in two minutes what the dug-up seeds showed over five days: the root first, then the curled shoot.
videos.check: Found by search: "Bean Time-Lapse - 25 days | Soil cross section" by GPhase, 3 minutes, 10 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.why: Real time-lapse of a pumpkin seed coming up, the round seed leaves opening, and the plant growing on. Watch the first part for the seedling.
videos.check: Found by search: "Pumpkin Growing from Seed to Flowers 🎃 120 days Time Lapse" by Seemingly Forever, 2 minutes, 58 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: What is seed germination? (Dr. Binocs)
videos.why: A simple cartoon explanation of how a seed wakes up and grows into a plant.
videos.check: Found by search: "What Is Seed Germination? | SEED GERMINATION | Plant Germination | Dr Binocs Show | Peekaboo Kidz" by Peekaboo Kidz, 6 minutes, 28 seconds. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: What grows out of a seed?
quiz.why: A seed holds a tiny baby plant. With water, the seed grows into a new plant.

quiz.p: What does a seed need to start growing?
quiz.why: A seed needs water to start growing. A dry seed waits.

quiz.p: Which part comes out of a seed first?
quiz.why: The root comes out first and grows down.

quiz.p: Which way does a root grow?
quiz.why: Roots grow down into the soil to drink water and hold on.
The shoot grows up. The stem and leaves come from the shoot.

quiz.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 1, plants a pumpkin seed. What will grow?
quiz.why: A seed grows into the same kind of plant the seed came from.

quiz.p: Why do we soak chana before planting?
opts: So the seed can drink water and start
To make the chana taste nice
quiz.why: Soaking gives the seed water, so the seed swells and starts to grow sooner.

quiz.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 1, plants seeds in a cup. What should she do every few days?
opts: Touch the soil and water if dry
Pour in water until the cup overflows
Put the cup in the fridge
quiz.why: Seeds need damp soil. Too much water makes them rot, so water only when the top is dry.

quiz.p: The shoot comes up bent over, like a finger. Why?
opts: So the soil does not scrape the soft tip
So the shoot can hide from the sun
quiz.why: The bent shoot pushes up with its back first, so the soft tip stays safe.

quiz.p: Where do pumpkin seeds come from?
quiz.why: A pumpkin holds many seeds. Each seed has a tiny baby pumpkin plant inside.

applications: Farmers sow seeds of rice, ragi and cotton when the soil is damp, often just as the monsoon rains come.
Families sprout moong, chana and methi in the kitchen to eat.
People plant mango, jackfruit and tamarind seeds to grow trees that give fruit for many years.
Seed banks keep seeds of many crops dry and cold, so the crops can be grown again in the future.

spotted.text: A small peepal or banyan plant growing out of a crack in a wall or on an old building, in almost any Indian city.
spotted.art: A small peepal plant with heart-shaped leaves growing out of a crack in an old city wall.

spotted.text: Moong sprouts with white tails in a steel bowl at home, or at a sundal stall in Chennai.
spotted.art: A steel bowl full of moong sprouts with short white tails.

spotted.text: Seed packets and seedlings in small black bags at a plant nursery on the roadside.
spotted.art: A roadside plant nursery with rows of small seedlings in black plastic bags.

spotted.text: Young green paddy seedlings in a nursery bed, before farmers in Andhra Pradesh, Bengal or Punjab plant them out in the fields.
spotted.art: A thick bed of young green rice seedlings, with a woman farmer lifting a bundle of them.

spotted.text: A tomato or chilli plant coming up in a pot from a seed in the kitchen waste, though nobody planted a seed there.
spotted.art: A balcony pot with a small tomato plant coming up next to the main plant.

open_questions.q: How does a seed know when the time is right to wake up?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that water, warmth and light can wake seeds. But how a seed weighs all of these together, and decides, is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How long can a seed stay alive and wait?
open_questions.why_open: Seeds can wait a very long time, but nobody knows the longest a seed can wait.

open_questions.q: What is it like for a root to feel the soil?
open_questions.why_open: Roots sense water, touch and which way is down, and they change where they grow. Nobody knows what that sensing is like for the plant.

ask_kids: Which seeds did you eat today? Could any of them grow?
When you see a plant on a wall, how did the seed get there?
If you were a seed, would you grow your root or your shoot first? Why?
Is the root of a pot plant at home bigger or smaller than the part we can see?
Where do the seeds in a papaya or a tomato go if nobody eats them?

jokes.j: Why did the seed stay in bed all morning?
jokes.a: Nobody gave them a drink to wake up!

jokes.j: Why did the root never get lost?
jokes.a: She always knew which way was down!

jokes.j: Why was the seed so good at hide and seek?
jokes.a: They grew their root where nobody could see!

jokes.j: Why did the chana stay in the bowl all night?
jokes.a: They were having a long bath!

jokes.j: Why did the shoot come up bent over?
jokes.a: To bow and say hello to the sunlight!

jokes.j: Why did the root go to every cricket match?
jokes.a: To root for the home team!

jokes.j: Why did the little seed get a gold star?
jokes.a: Because they came up with a great idea!

jokes.j: Where do seeds go to learn?

maths.problem: You planted 5 chana seeds. You dug up one each day for 4 days. How many seeds were never dug up?
maths.explain: 5 take away 4 is 1. That was seed 5, left to grow in the soil.
maths.context: This is about the five chana seeds in the Peek Under the Soil test.
maths.why_maths: Counting the seeds tells us which one was left in the soil.

maths.problem: Seed 2's root was 1 fingernail long. Seed 4's root was 5 fingernails long. How many fingernails longer was seed 4's root?
maths.explain: Count on from 1 to 5: 2, 3, 4, 5. That is 4 more fingernails.
maths.context: This is about the chana roots in the Peek Under the Soil test.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two lengths shows how much the root grew.

maths.problem: Imagine a test like Big Seed, Small Seed. On day 2, 6 moong had roots, but only 1 rajma did. Which kind sprouted faster? How many more moong had roots?
maths.answer: The moong sprouted faster. 5 more moong had roots.
maths.explain: 6 is more than 1. 6 take away 1 is 5.
maths.context: This is about the Big Seed, Small Seed test.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two numbers tells us which kind of seed was first, without guessing.

maths.problem: You counted 10 pumpkin seeds. You plant 4 of them in a cup. How many seeds are left to dry and keep?
maths.explain: 10 take away 4 is 6. You can check: 6 and 4 make 10.
maths.context: This is about the pumpkin seeds in What's in the Pumpkin? and the project Plant a Seed from Your Plate.
maths.why_maths: Taking away shows how many seeds we still have to plant later.

song.note: Topic-level song for Seeds and life cycles L1

links.why: For the parent: photograph a young plant growing out of a wall and find out their name.

buy.item: A small bag of potting soil or cocopeat
buy.why: For planting seeds if you have no pot plant to borrow soil from. Plant nurseries and online shops sell small bags cheaply.
buy.plan: Only needed if there is no soil at home. Soil from any existing pot works just as well.

warmup.q: Name two seeds that people eat.
warmup.a: For example chana, rajma, moong, rice or wheat.

warmup.q: What is inside a seed, besides the baby plant?
What will a mango stone grow into?

warmup.a: No. Only whole, raw seeds can sprout.
Yes. A dry seed is alive and waits for water.

founder: Week 7.0 'Let grow and grow': plant a seed, name the plant, water the plant and record progress. Used in the project, where the child names their plant.
science: Germination is completed when the radicle (embryonic root) emerges through the seed coat. In almost all flowering plants the radicle emerges before the shoot. Bewley and others, Seeds: Physiology of Development, Germination and Dormancy (Springer, 3rd edition 2013).
Dicot seedlings such as bean, chickpea and pumpkin push up through the soil with a bent hook (the apical hook), which protects the shoot tip and seed leaves.
Split pulses (dal) do not germinate because the embryo axis is damaged. Roasting kills the embryo.
Ficus seeds (peepal, banyan) are spread by birds and often sprout on walls and other trees. Ficus seeds are about 1 mm across.
Imbibition (soaking up water) is slower in larger seeds, so large seeds usually take longer to germinate, though the kind of seed also matters.

Sallon S. and others, Germination, genetics, and growth of an ancient date seed, Science 320 (2008): a date palm seed from Masada, dated to about 2,000 years ago, planted by Elaine Solowey in January 2005.
Cambridge Primary Science Stage 1, 2.2 Growing seeds.

roots.context: We planted chana, dug them up day by day, and saw what a seed does under the soil. Now we ask what that tells us about plants, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Our chana showed nothing above the soil for days. Under the soil, each one had already grown a root. A seed grows a root down first, to drink and hold on. Only then does the shoot come up into the light.
deep_truth.habit: We judge whether something is growing by what we can see. Above the soil nothing seemed to happen, yet the first days of a plant's life were busy underground.
deep_truth.evidence: In Peek Under the Soil, the dug-up seeds showed a root that got longer each day: a tiny tip on seed 1, a root as long as a fingernail on seed 2, and a long root on seed 3. A curled shoot came last.

three.who_am_i: You also grew out of sight, for nine months before you were born.
three.what_is_life: A living seed senses water and which way is down, and chooses where to grow, even in the dark.
three.what_is_this_world: Under every pot, field and forest, roots are growing where we cannot see. Much of the world's living happens out of sight.

roots.thread: A seed starts in the dark. The root senses which way is down and grows towards water. The shoot grows up towards the light. So one tiny seed becomes two parts going two ways, down into the soil and up into the air.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to break open a banyan fruit, and then one of its tiny seeds. Shvetaketu says he sees nothing inside. Uddalaka says the great banyan tree grows from that very fine thing which he cannot see.
teachings.link: Our chana showed nothing on top for days, yet a whole root was growing. A big plant starts from something too small, or too hidden, to see.

teachings.teaching: A tree as wide as your arms can reach grows from a tiny shoot. A journey of a thousand miles begins with one step.
teachings.link: Every big tree began as one small seed growing one small root. The start is small and slow, and it is still the start.

science.text: In almost all flowering plants, the root comes out of the seed first. Scientists use the root coming out as the sign that a seed has sprouted.
Roots sense which way is down, where water is, and what they touch, and they change where they grow. What that sensing is like for a plant, nobody knows yet.

other_view.view: Many plant scientists say a root grows down because of a fixed response to gravity that works the same way every time. They would not call this choosing.

practice.title: Feel your roots
practice.say: Stand still, with bare feet on the floor. Close your eyes. Press your feet down. Feel the floor pushing back. Now, very slowly, lift your arms up, like a shoot. Keep your feet pressed down. Breathe in, and breathe out. Your feet hold on, and your arms reach up.
practice.kid: Stand with bare feet. Close your eyes. Press your feet down. Slowly lift your arms up. Breathe in. Breathe out.

ask: If we had waited five days before looking, what would we have missed?
A tulsi on the balcony has roots too. Where are they, and what are they doing right now?
What did your chana need from you, and what did the chana do by itself?
roots.art: A child standing barefoot with arms raised, next to a cup of soil cut away to show a chana seedling with a long root going down and a shoot going up.

how_we_found_out.context: How long can a seed stay alive? This card tells the true story of a very old seed.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1960s, archaeologists digging at Masada, an old fort on a hill in Israel, found date seeds in a jar. The seeds were about 2,000 years old. Most people thought seeds that old must be long dead. The seeds sat in a drawer for about 40 years. Then a doctor and scientist, Sarah Sallon, wondered if they could still grow. She asked a plant scientist, Elaine Solowey, to try. In January 2005, Elaine Solowey soaked three of the seeds and planted them. After about eight weeks, one seed sent up a shoot. The team named the young date palm Methuselah, after a very old man in the Bible. Scientists tested a small piece of a leftover seed from the same place, and found the seed was about 2,000 years old. In 2008 the team wrote about it in the journal Science. At that time, Methuselah was the oldest seed ever known to grow into a plant. The tiny baby plant inside had stayed alive and waited for water for 2,000 years.
how_we_found_out.who: Sarah Sallon, a doctor and scientist, and Elaine Solowey, a plant scientist, in Israel
how_we_found_out.when: The seeds were found in the 1960s. Planted in January 2005. Reported in the journal Science in 2008.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That seeds thousands of years old must be dead. One 2,000-year-old date seed planted by Elaine Solowey sprouted and grew into a palm.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman in a greenhouse kneeling beside a small young date palm in a pot, with an old clay jar of seeds on a bench behind her.
